title: What is the G1 "humongous object" problem (object > 50% of region size), what issues does it cause (fragmentation, early GC pressure), and how do you fix it (bigger regions, smaller objects, switch to ZGC)?
shortTitle: The G1 humongous object problem — object larger than 50% of region size — what issues it causes, and how to fix it

s1_definition.profdef: In G1, any single object larger than half of a heap region is a "humongous object." It is not allocated in Eden; instead G1 reserves a run of contiguous Old regions to hold it, rounding up to whole regions. Humongous objects cause wasted space from rounding, cross-region fragmentation, and extra garbage-collection pressure because large humongous allocations can trigger concurrent cycles and, in older JDKs, were only reclaimed during certain collections.
s1_definition.analogy: The warehouse rooms are a fixed size. Most documents fit easily, but occasionally a customer submits one enormous ledger that is bigger than half a room. The rule says such a giant must get its own locked set of adjacent rooms, even if it only half-fills the last one, and those rooms cannot be shared. If giant ledgers keep arriving, the warehouse fragments into reserved chunks and the cleaning crew has to run extra inspections. That giant ledger is a humongous object.
s1_definition.oneliner: Any object bigger than half a G1 region becomes a humongous object that eats whole regions, wastes the remainder, and adds GC pressure.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In G1, any single object larger than half of a heap region is a "humongous object." It is not allocated in Eden; instead G1 reserves a run of contiguous Old regions to hold it, rounding up to whole regions. Humongous objects cause wasted space from rounding, cross-region fragmentation, and extra garbage-collection pressure because large humongous allocations can trigger concurrent cycles and, in older JDKs, were only reclaimed during certain collections.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The warehouse rooms are a fixed size. Most documents fit easily, but occasionally a customer submits one enormous ledger that is bigger than half a room. The rule says such a giant must get its own locked set of adjacent rooms, even if it only half-fills the last one, and those rooms cannot be shared. If giant ledgers keep arriving, the warehouse fragments into reserved chunks and the cleaning crew has to run extra inspections. That giant ledger is a humongous object.

**One line to remember:** Any object bigger than half a G1 region becomes a humongous object that eats whole regions, wastes the remainder, and adds GC pressure.

sections.s2_technical:
G1 region size is a power of two between one and thirty-two megabytes, chosen automatically from the heap size unless you set `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize`. The humongous threshold is exactly fifty percent of that region size. So with the common eight-megabyte region, any object larger than four megabytes is humongous. A single large byte array, a big cached document, or an oversized protobuf message can trip this.

Humongous objects are allocated directly into Old-generation regions as a contiguous run. If an object needs nine megabytes with eight-megabyte regions, it takes two regions and wastes nearly seven megabytes of the second region because nothing else may share humongous regions. That wasted tail is internal fragmentation.

The bigger pain is external fragmentation and GC pressure. To place a humongous object, G1 needs a contiguous run of free regions. If the heap is busy and free regions are scattered, G1 may fail to find a contiguous run and fall back to a Full GC to compact, which is the worst-case pause. Allocating many humongous objects can also repeatedly cross the IHOP threshold and kick off concurrent marking cycles far more often than the workload would otherwise need.

In older JDKs, humongous regions were only reclaimed at the end of a marking cycle or during mixed collections, so dead humongous objects could linger and inflate occupancy. Modern G1 reclaims eagerly dead humongous regions during young collections, which helps, but the fragmentation and contiguity problems remain.

The fixes, in order of preference. First, make the objects smaller — stream or chunk large payloads instead of holding one giant array, which is almost always the right production fix. Second, increase the region size with `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m` or `32m` so the object is no longer above the fifty-percent threshold; a sixteen-megabyte region makes the humongous threshold eight megabytes. Third, if large objects are genuinely intrinsic to the workload, switch to ZGC, whose region model and concurrent relocation handle large objects far more gracefully and whose pauses do not grow with heap or object size.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an end-of-day statement generator loads each customer's full annual transaction list into one big byte array to render a PDF. For heavy accounts these arrays are six to ten megabytes. On the default eight-megabyte regions, every one of these is a humongous object. This is exactly the humongous-object problem — objects over half a region each grab whole Old regions.

Problem 2 — During the nightly batch, thousands of these arrays are created and discarded. The heap fragments, G1 cannot always find contiguous free regions, and occasionally it falls back to a Full GC that freezes the batch for over a second. This is the fragmentation and GC-pressure symptom.

Our mini-project is a runnable demo that deliberately allocates humongous arrays and reports how many regions each would consume, demonstrates the "chunk it" fix that keeps every object under the threshold, and prints the flag-based fix. Classes are `StatementBatchSimulator` (driver), `StatementRenderer` (allocates big vs chunked), and `RegionMath` (computes region size, threshold, and whether an allocation is humongous).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
g1-humongous-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── run.sh
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/humongous/
            ├── StatementBatchSimulator.java   (main + demo classes)
            └── RegionMath.java
```

Configuration (JVM flags):

```bash
# humongous-fix.conf — three independent fixes, pick based on diagnosis
# Fix A: bigger regions so 8MB arrays are no longer humongous
-XX:+UseG1GC -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=32m
# Fix C: switch collector when large objects are intrinsic
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational
# Always: log GC and capture a heap dump on OOM
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,tags -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# Run on default 8MB regions — observe humongous warnings
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms1g -Xmx1g -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/g1-humongous-demo-1.0.0.jar \
     com.bank.jvm.humongous.StatementBatchSimulator

# Re-run with Fix A (bigger regions) and compare humongous allocation count
java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=32m -Xms1g -Xmx1g \
     -Xlog:gc+humongous=debug:file=gc-fix.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/g1-humongous-demo-1.0.0.jar \
     com.bank.jvm.humongous.StatementBatchSimulator

# Count humongous allocations G1 reported
grep -i humongous gc.log | wc -l
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a request to render Rajesh's statement needing nine megabytes of buffer, first as one array and then as chunks, on a JVM with eight-megabyte G1 regions.

Step 1. The simulator asks `RegionMath` for the region size and threshold. It computes region size eight megabytes and humongous threshold four megabytes and logs them.

Step 2. `renderBig` allocates one nine-megabyte array. Since nine is greater than four, `isHumongous` returns true. G1 cannot place this in Eden; it reserves a contiguous run of two Old regions (nine rounds up to sixteen megabytes) and wastes nearly seven megabytes in the second region.

Step 3. The data — the byte array contents — stays exactly as allocated, but its location is special: it occupies dedicated humongous regions rather than the normal Eden path. The gc log records a humongous allocation.

Step 4. `renderChunked` allocates the same nine megabytes as five chunks of two megabytes each (the last one megabyte). Every chunk is two megabytes or less, well under the four-megabyte threshold, so `isHumongous` is false for each. These land in ordinary Eden regions.

Step 5. When the chunks go out of scope, a normal young collection reclaims them cheaply with no need to find a contiguous run and no risk of a fragmentation-driven Full GC.

Step 6. The logs show the big path printing a humongous warning and a region count of two, while the chunked path prints humongous equals false for every chunk — the same payload, but one path stresses the collector and the other does not.

```
Oct 25, 2026 1:41:02 AM com.bank.jvm.humongous.StatementBatchSimulator main
INFO: Region size=8MB, humongous threshold=4MB
Oct 25, 2026 1:41:02 AM com.bank.jvm.humongous.StatementBatchSimulator main
WARNING: Rendering with ONE giant buffer per statement (humongous)
Oct 25, 2026 1:41:02 AM com.bank.jvm.humongous.StatementRenderer renderBig
WARNING: Statement SAV2001 buffer=9MB humongous=true consumes 2 whole region(s)
Oct 25, 2026 1:41:02 AM com.bank.jvm.humongous.StatementRenderer renderChunked
INFO: Chunk 2MB humongous=false
INFO: Statement SAV2001 rendered in 5 safe chunks
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Request: render SAV2001 statement = 9MB buffer
    │
    ├─ BIG PATH (one 9MB array)              ├─ CHUNKED PATH (5 × ~2MB)
    │   9MB > 4MB threshold → HUMONGOUS      │   each ≤ 2MB < 4MB → normal
    │   needs 2 contiguous Old regions       │   lands in Eden regions
    │   wastes ~7MB in 2nd region            │   no rounding waste
    │   may force Full GC if no run found    │   cheap young collection frees it
    ▼                                        ▼
  Fragmentation + GC pressure              Bounded, predictable pauses
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
In G1 a humongous object is any single object larger than half of a heap region. Region size is a power of two between one and thirty-two megabytes picked from the heap size, so on the common eight-megabyte region anything over four megabytes is humongous. These objects skip Eden entirely and are placed directly into a contiguous run of Old regions, rounded up to whole regions, which immediately wastes the tail of the last region as internal fragmentation.

The real damage is twofold. Because G1 needs a contiguous run of free regions to place a humongous object, a busy and fragmented heap can fail to find one and fall back to a Full GC to compact, which is the worst pause G1 can produce. And a stream of humongous allocations keeps crossing the initiating-occupancy threshold, kicking off concurrent marking cycles far more often than the workload really needs, so you pay in both latency spikes and wasted CPU.

I fix it in a defined order. First and best, I make the objects smaller — stream or chunk the large payload so no single allocation crosses the threshold, which is what I did at National Bank of India for the end-of-day statement generator that was holding each customer's whole annual history in one nine-megabyte array; splitting it into small chunks removed every humongous allocation and eliminated the occasional Full GC that was freezing the batch. If chunking is not feasible, I raise the region size, for example to thirty-two megabytes, so the threshold rises above the object size. And if large objects are genuinely intrinsic to the workload, I switch to ZGC, whose concurrent relocation handles large objects gracefully and whose pauses do not grow with object or heap size. I always confirm the fix by enabling the gc humongous debug log and alerting on any Full GC during the batch window.
